title: Survival Skills Academy
description: Essential outdoor, emergency, and life skills to keep you safe and self-reliant in any situation.

skills.title: Fire Safety & the Fire Triangle
skills.description: Fire needs three things: fuel (wood, paper), heat (spark, match), and oxygen (air). This is called the Fire Triangle. Remove any one side and fire cannot start or continue.
steps: Always have adult supervision around fire.
Keep a bucket of water or sand nearby before lighting any fire.
Never leave a fire unattended.
To extinguish: pour water over embers, stir, pour again until cold.
Check ashes are completely cold before leaving.
key_rules: Stop, Drop, Roll if clothing catches fire
Never use water on electrical or grease fires
Test doors with the back of your hand before opening during a house fire

quiz.q: What are the three elements of the Fire Triangle?
What should you do if your clothing catches fire?

skills.title: Finding Direction Without a Compass
skills.description: When lost without a compass, nature provides reliable direction clues. The Sun rises in the East and sets in the West. At noon in the Northern Hemisphere, the Sun is in the South. Moss on trees tends to grow on the cooler, shadier north side.
steps: Stick method: Push a stick into the ground. Mark the tip of its shadow.
Wait 15–20 minutes. Mark the new shadow tip.
Draw a line between the two marks. This runs roughly East–West.
The first mark is West, the second is East.
Stand with West to your left and East to your right — you are facing North.
key_rules: In the Southern Hemisphere, the Sun at noon is in the North
Stars: the North Star (Polaris) sits almost exactly above the North Pole
The Moon rises in the East and sets in the West like the Sun

quiz.q: Using the stick shadow method, the line drawn between two shadow tips runs:
Which star can help you find North in the Northern Hemisphere?

skills.title: Building Emergency Shelter
skills.description: In a survival situation, shelter is the first priority. You can die of hypothermia in hours if wet and cold, but survive weeks without food. A good shelter is small (body heat warms it), dry, and blocks wind.
steps: Find a natural windbreak (dense trees, rock face, hillside).
Lean long branches against a fallen log or low branch to form an A-frame.
Layer leaves, bark, and bracken over the frame from bottom to top (like roof tiles).
Make the layer at least 60 cm thick to insulate against rain and cold.
Fill the interior with dry leaves as bedding — insulates you from cold ground.
Keep the entrance small and facing away from prevailing wind.
key_rules: Ground insulation is as important as roof
Small shelter = warmer (body heats the air)
Never shelter under dead branches (widow-makers)

quiz.q: Why should a survival shelter be small?
options: Body heat warms a small space efficiently

skills.title: Finding and Purifying Water
skills.description: You can only survive about 3 days without water. Finding and making water safe to drink is a critical skill. Never drink untreated water from rivers or lakes — pathogens can cause severe illness.
steps: Follow valleys downhill — water flows downward.
Look for animal trails converging (they often lead to water).
Collect rainwater using leaves or tarpaulin funnelled into a container.
Boiling: bring water to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute (3 minutes at high altitude).
Improvised filter: layer grass, charcoal, sand, and gravel in a container. Water must still be boiled after filtering.
key_rules: Never drink seawater — it accelerates dehydration
Clear water can still contain pathogens
Morning dew can be collected from leaves using a cloth

quiz.q: How long should water be boiled to make it safe to drink (at sea level)?

skills.title: Using a Compass
skills.explanation: A compass always points magnetic north. Use it with a map to navigate.
steps: Hold the compass flat and let the needle settle.
Rotate the compass housing until N lines up with the needle.
Read the bearing you need to travel on.
Walk towards a landmark in that direction.
Check your bearing regularly.
skills.tip: Always double-check against landmarks — compasses can be affected by metal nearby.

quiz.question: Which direction does a compass needle point?
Why check landmarks when navigating?
options: To verify your compass bearing in real terrain

skills.title: Map Reading Basics
skills.explanation: Topographic maps show terrain height with contour lines and landmarks with symbols.
steps: Orient the map by turning it until features match the landscape.
Find your current location using two known landmarks (triangulation).
Read contour lines — close together means steep.
Measure distance using the map scale.
Plan a route avoiding hazards.
skills.tip: Contour lines that form a V pointing uphill show a valley; pointing downhill show a ridge.

quiz.question: Close contour lines on a map mean?
What is map triangulation?
options: Finding position using two known landmarks

skills.title: Reading the Weather
skills.explanation: Understanding cloud patterns and natural signs helps predict weather changes.
steps: Watch cloud types: cumulus (fair), cumulonimbus (storm), stratus (rain).
A red sky at night usually means fair weather ahead.
A red sky in the morning warns of approaching storms.
Rapidly falling pressure (if you have a barometer) indicates bad weather.
Wind direction shifts can signal incoming fronts.
skills.tip: Animals often behave differently before storms — insects disappear and birds fly low.

quiz.question: Cumulonimbus clouds usually indicate?
'Red sky at night' traditionally means?

skills.title: Choosing a Safe Campsite
skills.explanation: A good campsite provides shelter, safety, and access to resources.
steps: Avoid low ground — cold air and water collect there.
Stay away from dead trees or heavy branches overhead.
Choose ground that is slightly elevated and flat.
Stay 60 metres from water sources to protect them.
Look for natural windbreaks like rocks or dense shrubs.
skills.tip: Check for insect nests before settling. Avoid camping near ant trails.

quiz.question: Why avoid camping in low ground?
options: Cold air and water collect there

quiz.question: How far should a camp be from water?

skills.title: Essential Knots
skills.explanation: Knots are fundamental outdoor skills for building shelters, securing loads, and climbing.
steps: Reef knot: joining two ropes of similar thickness — left over right, then right over left.
Bowline: creates a fixed loop — 'the rabbit comes out of the hole, goes round the tree, back down the hole'.
Clove hitch: attaches rope to a pole or tree.
Figure-of-eight: stopper knot to prevent rope slipping through.
Practice each knot until you can tie it in the dark.
skills.tip: A knot that cannot be untied after use is called a 'hitch'; one that can be untied easily is a 'knot'.

quiz.question: A bowline creates?
Which knot joins two ropes of similar thickness?

skills.title: Making Water Safe to Drink
skills.explanation: In a survival situation, untreated water can carry diseases. Always purify water before drinking.
steps: Boiling: bring water to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute (3 minutes at altitude).
Filtration: pour through layers of cloth, sand, and charcoal to remove particles.
Purification tablets: follow package instructions — usually 1 tablet per litre.
UV pen: stir UV light in clear water for the prescribed time.
Solar disinfection (SODIS): fill a clear bottle and place in direct sun for 6+ hours.
skills.tip: Filtration removes particles but not all bacteria — always combine with boiling or tablets.

quiz.question: Minimum boiling time for safe water at sea level?
Does filtration alone make water fully safe?
options: No — combine with boiling or tablets

skills.title: Signalling for Help
skills.description: If lost, your priority is making yourself easy to find. The Rule of Three: three whistle blasts, three fires, three flashes of light are universal distress signals.
steps: Stay in one place if possible — easier for rescuers to find you.
Three whistle blasts, pause, repeat: international distress signal.
Mirror/shiny object: reflect sunlight toward planes or distant observers.
Ground signals: make a large X or SOS from stones or branches in an open area.
Smoke: add green leaves to fire for white smoke (visible against dark sky), rubber for black smoke (visible against light sky).
key_rules: SOS in Morse code: ... --- ...
Stay near your vehicle or tent — it's easier to spot
Bright colours attract attention — wave brightly coloured clothing

quiz.q: What is the universal distress signal using a whistle?

skills.title: Recognise and Treat Hypothermia
skills.description: Hypothermia happens when the body loses heat faster than it produces it, causing core temperature to drop below 35°C. It can be fatal. Early recognition is critical.
steps: Recognise signs: shivering, confusion, slurred speech, pale/blue skin, stumbling.
Move the person to shelter — out of wind and wet.
Remove wet clothing carefully and replace with dry layers.
Warm the core first (chest, armpits, groin) NOT hands and feet.
Give warm (not hot) drinks if conscious and able to swallow.
Wrap in blankets and insulate from the ground.
Call emergency services immediately for severe cases.
key_rules: Never rub limbs of a hypothermic person — can cause cardiac arrest
Give warm sweet drinks, not alcohol
Foil/space blankets reflect body heat back

quiz.q: Where should you warm a hypothermic person FIRST?

skills.title: Signalling for Rescue
skills.explanation: In an emergency, signalling rescuers quickly can save your life.
steps: International distress signal: three of anything — three whistles, three fires, three rocks.
Create a large ground-to-air signal: SOS in rocks or logs visible from the air.
Signal mirror: reflect sunlight towards aircraft using a mirror or shiny surface.
Stay near your last known location — easier for rescuers to find you.
A whistle is better than shouting — it carries further and uses less energy.
skills.tip: A personal locator beacon (PLB) is the most reliable emergency signal device.

quiz.question: International distress signal is?
Why stay near your last known location?
options: Easier for rescuers to search there

skills.title: Building an Emergency Shelter
skills.explanation: A shelter protects you from wind, rain, and cold — the biggest killers in survival situations.
steps: Find natural shelter first: caves, fallen trees, dense undergrowth.
A lean-to: prop a branch between two trees, rest branches against it, cover with leaves and debris.
Debris hut: build a ridge pole, prop sticks against it, pile leaves 1 metre thick all around.
Always insulate from the ground — more heat is lost downward than upward.
Keep your shelter small — body heat warms a small space much faster.
skills.tip: The debris hut can keep you warm in near-freezing temperatures using only your body heat.

quiz.question: Why insulate from the ground?
options: More heat is lost downward than upward

quiz.question: Why keep emergency shelters small?
options: Body heat warms small spaces faster

skills.title: Recognising and Treating Hypothermia
skills.explanation: Hypothermia occurs when body temperature drops dangerously low. It can kill if untreated.
steps: Signs: shivering, confusion, slurred speech, stumbling, pale skin.
Move the person to a dry, sheltered place immediately.
Remove wet clothing and replace with dry layers.
Warm the core first — chest, neck, groin — not the extremities.
Give warm (not hot) drinks if conscious. Seek medical help urgently.
skills.tip: Never give alcohol to a hypothermic person — it makes the body lose more heat.

quiz.question: First sign of hypothermia is usually?
Where should you warm a hypothermic person first?

skills.title: Wilderness First Aid Priorities
skills.explanation: When professional help is hours away, basic first aid knowledge is critical.
steps: Follow ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure.
Control heavy bleeding: apply firm, direct pressure for at least 10 minutes.
For a sprain: RICE — Rest, Ice (cold water), Compression, Elevation.
Suspected fracture: immobilise with a splint made from sticks and cloth.
Keep an injured person warm and still while sending for help.
skills.tip: Write down what happened, when, and what treatment was given — this helps medical teams.

quiz.question: RICE treatment is for?
For heavy bleeding apply?

skills.title: Lighting a Fire Safely
skills.explanation: Fire provides warmth, a way to purify water, signal rescuers, and cook food.
steps: Collect tinder (dry grass, bark, leaves), kindling (thin sticks), and fuel (larger logs).
Build a fire lay: teepee, log cabin, or star shape.
Use a lighter or matches — carry them in a waterproof bag.
Friction methods (bow drill, hand drill) work without matches but require practice.
Extinguish fully: douse with water, stir, repeat until cold to the touch.
skills.tip: Never leave a fire unattended. Clear flammable material in a 1-metre radius before lighting.

quiz.question: Tinder is?
options: Fine dry material to start a fire

quiz.question: How do you fully extinguish a fire?
options: Douse with water, stir, repeat until cold

skills.title: Safe Food Foraging Principles
skills.explanation: Wild food can supplement rations but requires careful identification to avoid poisoning.
steps: Never eat anything you cannot positively identify.
Learn the 'Universal Edibility Test' for unknown plants — takes 8 hours.
Safe plants in the UK: blackberries, nettles, hawthorn berries, elderberries (cooked only).
Avoid fungi unless you are an expert — many deadly species resemble edible ones.
Avoid plants with milky sap, bitter taste, or that smell of almonds.
skills.tip: When in doubt, don't. Starvation takes weeks; poisoning can kill in hours.

quiz.question: What is the Universal Edibility Test used for?
What feature may indicate a poisonous plant?

skills.title: Safe Foraging Rules
skills.description: Foraging means gathering wild food. NEVER eat anything you cannot identify with 100% certainty. Many edible plants have deadly lookalikes. Always use a field guide and learn from an expert first.
steps: The golden rule: If in doubt, don't eat it.
Learn three or four 100% identifiable plants in your region before foraging.
Check multiple features: leaf shape, stem, flower, smell, habitat.
Avoid foraging near roads (pollution), sprayed fields (pesticides), or polluted water.
Only take what you need — leave enough for wildlife and plant regeneration.
key_rules: Dangerous lookalikes: Wild hemlock looks like cow parsley (hemlock is deadly)
Deadly nightshade berries look like elderberries
Never forage fungi unless trained — many deadly mushrooms look edible

quiz.q: What is the golden rule of foraging?
options: If in doubt, don't eat it

skills.title: Widely Identifiable Safe Plants
skills.description: These are among the most reliably identifiable and widely distributed edible wild plants — but always learn from an expert in person first.
steps: Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale): entire plant edible — leaves, flowers, root. Toothed leaves, hollow stem with milky sap, distinctive yellow flower.
Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus): unmistakable thorny bramble with black compound fruits in late summer.
Nettles (Urtica dioica): sting when raw, but cooking destroys sting. Rich in iron and vitamins. Use gloves to pick.
Clover (Trifolium): three-leafed plant with round flower heads. Flowers and leaves edible raw.
key_rules: Always wash foraged plants before eating
Start with very small quantities in case of individual sensitivity
Inform an adult of everything you eat while foraging

quiz.q: Which common plant has the distinctive feature of hollow stem with milky sap and toothed leaves?

skills.title: Common Edible Wild Plants (UK)
skills.explanation: Learning to identify edible plants builds confidence and could save your life.
steps: Stinging nettles: edible after cooking or blanching, rich in iron and vitamin C.
Blackberries: dark purple berries in hedgerows from August-October.
Hawthorn berries: small red berries, best cooked into jams.
Wood sorrel: small heart-shaped leaves with a lemony taste, good in salads.
Dandelion: leaves (bitter salad), flowers (garnish), roots (roasted coffee substitute).
skills.tip: Always wash wild plants thoroughly before eating. Pick away from roadsides.

quiz.question: Nettles are safe to eat after?
When are blackberries typically ripe in the UK?

skills.title: Animal Tracking Basics
skills.explanation: Reading animal signs helps you understand your environment and find resources.
steps: Look for footprints in soft mud — count toes to identify the animal.
Droppings (scat) indicate what animals live and eat nearby.
Nibbled leaves or bark show browsing mammals.
Feathers, fur, or bones indicate predator activity.
Follow well-worn animal trails — they often lead to water.
skills.tip: Deer trails through undergrowth are often the easiest paths in dense forest.

quiz.question: What does scat tell you?
options: What animals live nearby and their diet

quiz.question: Why follow animal trails in dense forest?
options: They are usually easiest paths and lead to water

skills.title: Navigating by Nature
skills.explanation: Before compasses, people navigated using the sun, stars, and natural signs.
steps: Sun: rises in the east, sets in the west — south at noon in the Northern Hemisphere.
Stars: the North Star (Polaris) is above true north; find it via the Plough constellation.
Moss: often grows on the north side of trees and rocks (more shade there).
Tree rings: trees grow more on the south side (more sun) — wider rings on that side.
Shadow stick: place a stick vertically; mark tip of shadow; wait 15 minutes; mark again. The line between marks runs roughly east-west.
skills.tip: The moss/tree ring methods are rough guides — always confirm with other clues.

quiz.question: Where is the sun at midday in the Northern Hemisphere?
How do you find north using the Plough?
options: Follow the pointer stars to Polaris

skills.title: Finding Water in the Wild
skills.explanation: The human body can survive only 3 days without water. Finding it is a top priority.
steps: Follow valleys downhill — water flows to lower ground.
Listen for running water, especially in quiet forests.
Look for lush green vegetation in otherwise dry terrain.
Animal trails and bird flight paths often lead to water sources.
Collect morning dew by wiping long grass with absorbent cloth, then wring it out.
skills.tip: Never drink seawater — it causes rapid dehydration.

quiz.question: Which direction does water flow?
How can you collect water in the morning?
options: Collect dew from grass with cloth

skills.title: Identifying Dangerous Plants and Insects
skills.explanation: Knowing what to avoid is as important as knowing what is edible or harmless.
steps: Deadly Nightshade: shiny black berries, dull leaves — extremely toxic.
Giant Hogweed: large white flower clusters — causes severe skin burns in sunlight.
Hemlock: hollow stems, white flowers, musty smell — extremely toxic.
Wasps and bees: do not swat — back away calmly; swatting triggers attack.
Ticks: after outdoor activities, check skin folds for ticks; remove with fine tweezers.
skills.tip: If stung by many bees/wasps and showing signs of allergic reaction (swelling, difficulty breathing), call 999 immediately.

quiz.question: Giant Hogweed is dangerous because?
options: Its sap causes severe burns in sunlight

quiz.question: How should you react to a nearby wasp?

skills.title: Staying Calm in Emergencies
skills.description: In a survival situation, panic kills. It causes poor decisions, wastes energy, and makes small problems worse. The STOP method is used by military and rescue professionals worldwide.
steps: S — Stop: Do not run, do not panic. Sit down if possible.
T — Think: What is my immediate danger? What resources do I have?
O — Observe: Look around. Where is shelter? Which way is downhill? Is anyone nearby?
P — Plan: Make a simple plan for the next 1–2 hours only. Act on it.
key_rules: Fear is normal and useful — it sharpens your senses
Slow breathing (4 counts in, 4 hold, 4 out) activates the body's calm response
Singing, talking to yourself, or counting helps prevent panic

quiz.q: In the STOP method, what does the 'O' stand for?

skills.title: Managing Stress and Fear
skills.explanation: Fear and panic are your biggest enemies in a survival situation. Managing them keeps you thinking clearly.
steps: Acknowledge fear — it is a normal, helpful response.
Use box breathing: inhale 4s, hold 4s, exhale 4s, hold 4s.
Repeat a calming phrase: 'I can handle this one step at a time.'
Focus on immediate small actions — collect water, build shelter.
Remember the rule of threes: 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without warmth, 3 days without water, 3 weeks without food.
skills.tip: Action beats anxiety. Doing something useful immediately lowers fear levels.

quiz.question: What is box breathing?
The rule of threes says you need warmth within?

skills.title: Decision-Making Under Pressure
skills.explanation: Good decisions in survival require slowing down, assessing the situation, and prioritising.
steps: STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan.
List your resources: what do you have?
Prioritise using rule of threes (air, warmth, water, food).
Make a simple plan — don't over-complicate.
Review the plan after each step and adapt.
skills.tip: Most survival mistakes happen from acting too quickly. STOP and think first.

quiz.question: What does STOP stand for?
options: Stop, Tell someone, Organise, Push on

quiz.question: What is the first priority in a survival situation?

skills.title: Developing a Positive Mental Attitude
skills.explanation: Survivors consistently report that attitude — the will to survive — is the single biggest factor.
steps: Set small, achievable goals ('I will collect water in the next 20 minutes').
Celebrate small wins — every achieved goal builds confidence.
Visualise a positive outcome.
Connect to your 'why' — family, responsibilities, dreams.
Avoid negative self-talk ('I can't do this') — reframe ('This is hard but I will try').
skills.tip: Survivors who kept a routine — even simple tasks — showed much better mental resilience.

quiz.question: Why set small goals in a survival situation?
options: Each small win builds confidence and focus

quiz.question: Reframing means?
options: Changing the physical frame of reference
Replacing negative thoughts with constructive ones

skills.title: Handling Boredom and Isolation
skills.explanation: Long survival situations can lead to boredom, loneliness, and psychological breakdown.
steps: Create a daily routine — wake time, tasks, rest, sleep.
Keep a journal or make notes/drawings in the dirt.
Talk out loud to yourself — process thoughts and stay mentally sharp.
Set daily improvement targets: make the shelter better, find more food.
Remember that rescue teams will be searching — stay hopeful.
skills.tip: People who maintain routines in isolation show significantly better psychological health.

quiz.question: Why create a daily routine in survival?
options: Routine maintains mental health and focus

quiz.question: Talking out loud to yourself in isolation helps because?
options: It processes thoughts and maintains mental sharpness

skills.title: Helping Others in an Emergency
skills.explanation: Group survival is nearly always more effective than surviving alone.
steps: Assess each person's physical and mental state quickly.
Assign tasks based on ability — everyone contributes.
Keep group morale high — acknowledge effort and achievement.
Look after the most vulnerable first: injured, elderly, children.
Share resources fairly and openly to build trust.
skills.tip: Groups with a clear, calm leader and fair decision-making survive at much higher rates.

quiz.question: In a group survival situation, who should be cared for first?
options: The most vulnerable — injured, elderly, children

quiz.question: What is the key benefit of group survival?
